chapter: Joseph Thomas band and house parties
title: Bass, trombone and piano players in the Thomas band
summary: Williams tries to name the band's bass player, trombonist Eddie Summers and pianist Joe Lewis, then remarks on the union changing as rock and roll kids join.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: That's funny, I never heard of him. But he, and let's see, did you have a bass player, a trombone player?
A bass player died. P.T. I don't know him. He was a big fellow, he was a painter, tall, very fat.
That was his last name? Yeah. I heard of Joe P.T. and Buddy P.T. and T.E.T. Roussone.
P.T. And trombone or saxophone? He was a bass player. Did you have a trombone?
Who did I? In that band with Coyne Brad? Oh, sometime, Eddie Summers, that's his, I used to use Eddie Summers. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Did you ever use a piano?

Oh, sometime, Eddie Summers, that's his, I used to use Eddie Summers. You ever use a piano? Piano, yeah. We use a piano. Now this boy, I see this boy all the time and I can't think of his name. He's old. Joe Lewis. He's a Dixieland fool.
I don't know Joe Lewis. I know Walter Lewis. Little bit of Brownskins, brother. Stay back on Pearl Street. Oh, I don't know where he lives. It might be the same guy that might
have two names. He drinks a whole lot. That's him. That was his regular piano. That was Thomas' regular piano player. We called him Joe Lewis, all in the
history of the life. Joe Lewis was a popular name about that time.

Yeah. Played plenty of piano, Dixieland man. He figured he plays a lot of jobs now that he figured he'd come back in the union. Oh, he'd play on any kind of old broken piano. He'd put you in mind of Mitchell Fridge in there. Played all over the Bad Keys. Doesn't worry, man. No. Well, anyway. And sometimes they used to use
little Sammy Hopton. Mm-hmm. But I hardly see him anymore.

He's interesting. I saw him about a monocle. You see what is happening now, that union is kind of breaking up some of them fellas now. They're getting away, because the majority of the boys in school, they're all coming in local. Little rock and roll fellas, you know what I mean? They're coming in local. This little kid used to play so much climate, I started him off. He's a music major. Leonard Eberidge. I used to use him in the brass band, young kid. Well, is he Ken does something? Is that something? Step Daddy or something? Is that the one? No, he don't. No, he have a brother playing up there in Tuskegee. I mean, not Tuskegee, I know. Southern. But he didn't finish him. He's teaching. Leonard Eberidge. Yeah, well, I've seen him. See, he used to give me permission to use him. Otherwise, we used to be real lean on the schools. We gave the school children a lot of breaks. And sometimes in the summer time, in the carnival time, I had to use very few men's in the city. I'd send home. And I'd get this boy, Emory, Big Emory, first of the hundred brothers. He was up there in college. How many times did he get? Yeah, he'd bring, because he was going to make ten or fifteen, twenty dollars, you know, for himself. And boy, he'd bring them down. He'd bring them down. He'd bring them down. He'd get them down. And he'd call me, you know, from up there. He'd say, I'm on my way. Anything we wanted to get, that was it. And he'd bring more men that he needed. Down from Southern. From Southern. And then when I used to pay off, I'd pay him off. Then And then when I used to pay off, I'd pay him off. Then he'd pay them off. But I had them hired for thirty-five dollars, thirty-five dollars a man. Poor Bob was up there broke and saw me, they had a dime in their pocket. They was glad to get on there for fifteen or twenty dollars. To get back on the campus, we'd have something to go back on the campus with.
